title: Texas Republican's post on Asian Americans at UT Austin sparks accusations of racism
description: -Nuño WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - A Republican nominee for a Texas office drew bipartisan criticism after posting a photo from a University of Texas football game that critics called
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - A Republican nominee for a Texas office drew bipartisan criticism after posting a photo from a University of Texas football game that critics called racist, portraying the Austin campus as dominated by foreign students contrary to enrollment data.

Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, drew a ‌sharp rebuke from fellow Republicans as well as Democrats after posting a crowd shot at a University of Texas football game, while suggesting that what appeared to be ‌students of South Asian descent reflected a large foreign-born or international student presence on campus.

"I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," French posted ​to his X account. He went on to claim that UT prioritizes foreign students in admissions and feared Texans were losing opportunities at the university.

"I weep for the families in Texas who can't get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans," he said.

But enrollment figures released by the University of Texas at Austin show international students account for less than 10% of the total student body. Total enrollment reached 55,000 students for the fall 2025 semester, including 5,140 international students. Texas residents make up 80.5% of all enrolled students.

For the undergraduate class, international students make up 4.3%, and a state law requires ‌90% of every incoming freshman class to be Texas residents. UT ⁠Austin automatically admits the top 5% of performers — who are also Texas residents — at every high school in the state.

The Texas legislature designed the initiative to promote diversity without explicitly considering race. As in most of the country, Texas high school students are separated by geography, income and demographics, and ⁠by guaranteeing admission to top students at each high school, the statewide policy helps ensure universities draw from a broad cross-section of Texas communities.

That means more than 90% of students at UT Austin are domestic, and more than four out of every five are Texans.

Vedant Nair, 24, who graduated from UT in 2024, said his parents immigrated to Oklahoma in the 1990s from Mumbai so his father could pursue an MBA ​at ​Oklahoma State University. Nair was born in Oklahoma City and recalls running around in a child-size OSU Cowboys ​football helmet and driving a mini John Deere tractor. His upbringing, he ‌said, was no different than those of his fellow Texans after his family moved to Dallas in elementary school.

Attending UT Austin was a dream come true, and a normal, American experience, he said.

"If you stripped away my name and skin color, I think my story is pretty similar to a lot of other Texans at massive public high schools," Nair said. "The point is that myself, and all the other kids in that picture, are just regular American kids."

University spokespeople and French did not respond to a request for comment.

The debate touches on a broader political argument that non-U.S. citizens are "displacing" American students at elite public universities, and the country at large.

French's remarks drew criticism from political figures and other social media users, who characterized the posts as racist or xenophobic.

Rodney ‌Coates, a sociology professor at Miami University in Ohio, said French's comments echoed longstanding anti-immigrant and anti-Asian narratives ​in the U.S. that have historically portrayed minority groups as threats to opportunities for others.

"It's easier to come up ​with a racist argument to organize a group of people under the presumption that, ​hey, they're hurting your chances," Coates said. Such appeals often have little to do with the people being targeted and instead seek to mobilize voters ‌by portraying them as victims. "Hate is one of the easiest means of ​organizing," he said.

University figures show white students made up ​about 31.5% of enrollment in 2024 to 2025, Hispanic students 25.5% and Asian students 22.4%.

University reporting treats race and ethnicity separately from international student status, meaning most students categorized as Asian are U.S. citizens or permanent residents rather than international students.

The image French shared was a screenshot from a video posted by the official athletics account at UT Austin. He did ​not include information identifying the citizenship, immigration status, residency or enrollment ‌status of any individuals shown.

For Nair, the unfortunate part of French's post was that it criticized a high point in school-pride history: the football team defeated The ​Ohio State University, the No. 1-ranked football team in the country.

"I don't think there is anything more American than people in cowboy hats yelling their heads off ​after one of the greatest comeback wins in college football history," he said.

title: Will Stein admits he was conservative on offense in Alabama loss
description: The Cats will aim to move the offense in the right direction when they travel to Texas A&M on Saturday.
fullText:
Kentucky Football fans entered year one of the Will Stein era optimistic and eager to see a new, more exciting brand of football at Kroger Field.

This offseason, the BBN shared a collective sentiment centered heavily on the simple eye test. It's fair to say most UK fans have approached this season with a focus that goes beyond simply tallying wins and losses.

For all the good Mark Stoops did for the Kentucky football program, his offensive approach didn't exactly make for must‑see TV. So the introduction of Will Stein's playbook became one of, if not the, biggest reasons to bring him to Lexington.

The stage was set Saturday when Kentucky hosted Alabama, offering a true benchmark for where this team stood offensively. The results were tough to swallow.

Aside from a few first‑half flashes, Kenny Minchey struggled to generate much under center against the Crimson Tide. Explosive plays were nearly nonexistent, prompting head coach Will Stein to address the lack of offensive production fans are craving.

"We've got to be able to generate and create explosive plays. I think that's obvious," Stein stated during his Tuesday press conference.

Stein went on to explain that he wanted to stay conservative in key moments, but that isn't something he and offensive coordinator Joe Sloan want to do.

"There were specific times in the game that I felt like we could have taken those punches," said Stein about going for more aggressive plays. "And that's not a Joe Sloan problem. That's a me problem. So what can I do as a head coach in those moments to give our players and give our coaches that type of confidence to go out there and swing when we have a chance?"

It's encouraging to see that, even after reflection, the goal remains to put it all on the line and try to win the football game — even against a powerhouse like Alabama.

Stein and his staff won't have to wait long to put that mindset into practice. They'll face one of the toughest challenges in college football this weekend when they travel to No. 9 Texas A&M. It's unfair to make firm assertions with only eight quarters of game film to go on, but there's no denying that another poor showing for the offense this weekend and things could begin to spiral.

title: Holly Rowe reveals private talk with Arch Manning after AI video backlash

Texas Longhorns star quarterback Arch Manning published an apology on Tuesday afternoon following his response to a viral AI video that depicted his head coach slapping a female journalist.

Manning's apology focused on his back-and-forth with reporters on Monday about a social media post featuring an AI-generated video showing Longhorns head coach Sarkisian slapping ESPN reporter Holly Rowe, and Manning was asked if he'd seen it.

"I saw an AI edit of Sark's interview," Manning said, laughing. "That's a good one - of him slapping Holly Rowe. That's hilarious."

After morning practice, Manning took to Instagram stories to make his apology public.

"In my press conference yesterday, I made an insensitive comment about an AI video," Manning's statement reads. "There is nothing funny about it. Rowe responded to Manning's post on Instagram, acknowledging the apology and sharing that the two had a conversation about the matter.

"Thank you Arch. I appreciate our conversation about this, which will remain private. Apology accepted," Rowe replied on Instagram. "We move forward with respect and kindness for one another."

Manning, 22, is currently the star junior quarterback for a Longhorns team that just moved up to No. 1 in the AP Top 25 Poll on Monday. Peyton and Eli Manning's nephew will hopefully have better, more mature days on the microphone in future press conferences.

title: Texas Republicans are scrambling after Bo French’s outburst
description: GOP operatives fear Bo French’s rhetoric could undermine the party’s recent gains with Hispanic and Asian American voters.
fullText:
Texas Republicans were already fretting about slipping support with voters of color. Then Bo French got on X.

The Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner posted a photo of a crowd of University of Texas football fans, most of them people of color, saying, "The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined." The Sunday morning comments, which appeared to target South Asian students, sent Lone Star Republicans into a frenzy, worried about the impact the rhetoric could have on GOP candidates up and down the ballot, including Attorney General Ken Paxton's high-profile Senate race and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection fight.

A number of Republican lawmakers, including some in tough races, quickly denounced the post as racist, as others squirmed with carefully worded statements. And GOP operatives winced at the potential electoral backlash — in a year that's already looking tougher-than-normal for a party that has dominated the state for decades. Still, no one explicitly called for him to drop out of the race.

"His post on social media is profoundly unhelpful if his goal is to see Republicans win statewide races in a tough political environment in 50 days," said Matt Mackowiak, an Austin-based GOP consultant who advised Sen. John Cornyn's (R-Texas) unsuccessful primary campaign against Paxton.

Cornyn condemned the post, asking whether other GOP officials would "condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized."

Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas), who is facing a tough reelection fight in a Hispanic-majority district, told POLITICO in a statement she's willing to "condemn racism" wherever it comes from.

"All I see in that photograph is a group of kids celebrating a Longhorns win. What can be more Texan than that?" De La Cruz said, before taking a shot at her Democratic opponent, Bobby Pulido, for his past racial comments.

And Karl Rove, a longtime adviser to former President George W. Bush, called French a "bigot" at a private lunch event and said he's voting for French's Democratic opponent, The Texas Tribune reported. Meanwhile, state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat running against French, said he had his best fundraising day of the cycle after French's post.

French didn't respond to requests for comment. He repeatedly stood by his comments since Sunday morning. During a local radio appearance Monday, he said he didn't have any personal animosity against the students at the football game, but said that it is "not racist to point out that we should be favoring Texans over foreigners" and that his fellow Republicans are afraid of being called racist.

The divide emerging among Texas Republicans over the social media post — and Democrats' eagerness to capitalize on it — show just how precarious the party finds its position this cycle. Texas Republicans were already worrying about losing support from Hispanic and other minority voters amid a tough economic environment and President Donald Trump's unpopular immigration agenda. They need to hold onto or improve the incremental gains they made over previous cycles with voters of color in a fast-changing state where non-Hispanic white people now only make up 37% of the population. The stakes are high this cycle: Most polls show Paxton slightly trailing in a Senate race that could determine control of the upper chamber; Abbott appears to be in the toughest of his four election fights; and the state is home to several key House races.

"I don't think [French's post] independently and universally sours voter sentiment. But it contributes to GOP declining numbers with Hispanic voters particularly in the South Texas congressional races which we hope to win," said Alfredo Rodriguez, a Dallas-based Republican strategist, who called on French to "stop the petty political theatrics."

The blast radius of French's posts was wide enough to garner carefully worded responses from the top of the ticket. Abbott said in a Sunday statement that French's post "is not my message," before noting unity "doesn't mean that Texas cannot also lead in having the toughest immigration laws of any state in America and freezing H1B visas at our universities."

Two of the students in the photo told the Dallas Morning News that they're U.S. citizens. Most UT students are Texans — state law requires that 90% of each freshman class come from in-state — and there is no evidence that the students in the photo French posted are foreigners.

Some Republicans weren't thrilled about Abbott's response.

"This had nothing to do with illegal immigrants," said Anang Mittal, an Indian American national GOP strategist, of Abbott's comments. "These were students at a college game. They're not H-1B. If they're students, they're on a student visa. … It's pretty damn disgusting of Greg Abbott to say, 'I condemn racism, but also, like, we're keeping all the Indians out.' That's essentially what that tweet read to me."Democrat James Talarico called Paxton out on social media, asking if he would follow Cornyn's lead in denouncing French's post. The GOP nominee replied that he condemns "racism in all its forms" — and then claimed Talarico had a "history of dividing Texans by race."

Spokespeople for Paxton and Abbott did not respond to requests for comment.

Other Republicans were less willing to fully denounce French's comments.

"I don't really know the guy. I heard he said some not so pleasant things," said Rep. Troy Nehls (R-Texas), who said he hadn't seen the posts — but launched into a criticism of immigration nonetheless. "I am concerned about the number of people living in this country, and we don't even know who they really are," he said. "Shut the border down for 10 years, and then let's try to figure out who we got in this country because we don't even know."

Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.), who campaigned with Talarico in Houston on Sunday, said French's posts came up in conversations with every Asian American voter he met.

"Everyone was talking about it," Kim said. "Every single Asian American that I was with yesterday raised this with me. They were saying this is an example of, 'Not only are they not courting us or engaging with us, but they're actively demonizing us, actively being xenophobic and racist towards us.' We need leaders that stand up against this."

The political damage could also extend — potentially for years — to Texas' small but growing Indian American population, the demographic group French appeared to target in his posts. Both Dallas and Houston have significant Indian American populations. In 2019, an event at a Houston stadium headlined by Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi drew over 50,000 attendees.

French's comments could alienate those same voters, said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican consultant in Austin.

"He just irritated a bunch of people, many of whom could be supporters and could be Republicans," said Steinhauser, a University of Texas graduate. "I'd be willing to bet a lot of those kids that he was posting a photo of are probably, you know, their parents might be Republicans, or they might be Republicans, or conservatives, or independent-leaning conservatives."

If French is elected, he would sit on a commission that regulates Texas' powerful oil, gas and mining industries — which has little to do with immigration or social issues. But French, a longtime provocateur in Texas political circles, has a history of incendiary statements. Just last year, Republicans were calling on French to resign as chair of the Tarrant County Republican Party after he published an online poll asking whether Muslims or Jews were "the bigger threat to America." He deleted the post and said he regretted it, adding "antisemitism has no place in the Republican Party." This spring, he unseated a well-financed Republican incumbent for Texas Railroad Commission.

French isn't the only politician in Texas who has made singling out Muslims part of his political brand. Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick has made "preventing Shariah law in Texas" one of his legislative priorities. Patrick didn't respond to a request for comment. Abbott, Paxton and Cornyn have all called for investigations and other government action to stop development of a commercial and residential development being built by the East Plano Islamic Center, a mosque outside Dallas. And just last month, Abbott threatened to withhold funding from Dallas Fort Worth International Airport to block plans for ritual washing facilities for Muslim travelers in the airport's terminals. There's little difference between French's attacks and the other politicians' actions, said Yasir Qadhi, an Islamic scholar at the Islamic center."It is the same mindset," he said in an interview. "What we're witnessing is really an unprecedented and increasingly brazen form of racism. It's unfiltered, it's unapologetic, it's even stripped of even the pretense of political correctness. You know, this is a type of racism we've never seen in our lifetimes."

When French unleashed a string of inflammatory social media posts in 2025, several GOP officeholders — including Patrick, the lieutenant governor — called on him to resign as county GOP chair. But Republicans now refuse to tell French to drop out now "because that might mean that there would be a Democrat elected statewide," said Glen Whitley, a Republican former Tarrant County judge. "That's the bottom line."

"That's part of my frustration with the Republican Party altogether: They talk about being Christian, but they get up every morning to talk about who they hate," said Whitley, who still identifies as Republican but endorsed Talarico for Senate.

Joey Fox contributed to this report.

title: Unearthed clip shows Talarico calling parents 'abusive' for denying children's gender identity

fullText:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once described parents who refused to acknowledge their children's gender identity as potentially engaging in "abusive" behavior.

"I think there are some folks that would think that if you deny your child's gender identity, that's incredibly harmful. And whether or not we label it with the term abuse, it's abusive for sure," Talarico said while speaking at a committee hearing in the Texas Legislature in 2019.

Talarico's resurfaced comments add to a growing pile of past remarks that cut against his efforts to paint himself as a moderate on issues like gender, policing and border security as he attempts to win over Texas, a historically Republican-leaning state.

Talarico Says He 'Missed The Mark' As He Backtracks On Controversial Woke Statements

The legislation aimed to ensure that parents who refused to affirm their child's gender identity would not be considered guilty of child abuse in cases deciding custody.

"In determining whether to appoint a party as a sole or joint managing conservator of a child, the court may not consider evidence regarding whether the party demonstrates a history or pattern of acknowledging or declining to acknowledge the child's gender identity or expression," its text read.

Talarico opposed the bill, arguing that he would not rule out an overlap: that, in some cases, the lack of acknowledgment could border on abuse.

"My concern is ruling it out as not being abuse, I think, is dangerous and could certainly harm some of our most vulnerable kids in the state."

"Only perverts and pedophiles think about what is in little kids' pants as much as James Talafreako. He is a truly sick individual for dedicating his life to pushing sex changes on other people's kids," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Republican Greg Abbott says datacenters must help ‘protect’ drought-prone state and disclose water use

Greg Abbott, the Texas governor, has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use.

“Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water,” the Republican governor said on Monday. “The Texas Water Code requires a complete and accurate water use survey. I direct the Texas Water Development Board to use its enforcement authority to penalize past failures and to impose legal consequences for any future failure to comply,” he added.

In a letter to the water board, Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, said: “Major water users, including data centers, appear to have committed civil and criminal violations by failing to provide the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) with information about water usage as required by the Texas Water Code.”

It follows a directive Abbott issued last month ordering the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (Ercot) to conduct a comprehensive audit of datacenters advancing through the Ercot interconnection process.

Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom.

Texas has the second-most datacenters of any state in the country, according to a tally by the Pew Research Center. But with 335 datacenters, and at least 248 

But, amid growing public concern over datacenter construction, Texas has been working to tighten oversight of the industry as demand grows for the state’s power and water supplies.

In 2025, Texas datacenters consumed an estimated 25bn gallons of water, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center. Water use by datacenters in the state could rise to 161bn gallons a year by 2030 – about 2.7% of all water used in Texas, or roughly the amount consumed by 1.3m households across the country.

The audit requires datacenters to provide information about their water consumption, water sources and efforts to use water-efficient technologies. Abbott said projects that fail to complete the audit will be denied permission to connect to the state’s power grid.

“TWDB’s water use surveys serve a similarly important purpose as this data center audit. TWDB must coordinate with PUC and ERCOT to ensure that covered entities provide critical water use information in response,” Abbott said in his Monday letter. “Any failure to respond to the audit’s request for water use information would trigger TWDB’s independent enforcement authority.”

title: Texas Senator Ted Cruz pitches Protect College Sports Act on College GameDay, warns against what will happen without action
description: Senator Ted Cruz sent a dire warning if Congress does not pass the Protect College Sports Act. In about five years, in Cruz’s estimation, football and other sports will be in an unrecognizable state. The biggest things for Cruz are the transfer rules and a hard out on eligibility for college athletes. You get one […]
fullText:
Senator Ted Cruz sent a dire warning if Congress does not pass the Protect College Sports Act. In about five years, in Cruz's estimation, football and other sports will be in an unrecognizable state.

The biggest things for Cruz are the transfer rules and a hard out on eligibility for college athletes. You get one free transfer and five years of eligibility in total, which ends regardless of how many years used once you turn the age of 24. Keeping that in place, along with an even playing field when it comes to NIL, this is the best solution for football, basketball, wone's sports and other Olympic sports, per Cruz.

$19.99 gets you a FULL year of On3 | Rivals national coverage

"There are no rules, and the situation with the transfer portal, where kids go and transfer two, three, four, five times, it's terrible for the game. It's terrible for the players. It's terrible for the schools, and it's terrible for the families," Cruz said on College GameDay. "And so the reason Congress is acting is because Congress created this problem. It was the federal antitrust laws that were used to bring the lawsuits that struck down all the rules, and so the Protect College Sports Act is bipartisan legislation that's very simple.

"It brings order to chaos. It protects the students, protects the student's ability to be compensated to receive name, image, and likeness compensation, I think that's only fair. It's only right."

Cruz is all about NIL and athletes getting compensated what they're worth. However, that's the key phrase. What they're worth and that has to do with revenue sharing and essentially the limitation of a blank checkbook.

"They're producing enormous value with an enormous skill, but it also puts reasonable rules in place," Cruz said. "So, for example, every player gets one free (transfer), not three or five, one (transfer). It puts an eligibility rule that every player has five years of eligibility, not six, seven, eight; five. And it puts a hard end on that at age 24. It lets the schools compete, and it also slows down what we've got right now (which) is a spiral of cost that is bankrupting almost every college program, most college athletic programs.

"They're losing 10s of millions of dollars, and as a result, they're canceling women's programs. They're canceling non-revenue sports. They're canceling Olympic sports. Within three to five years, we're going to see 40 to 50 schools that have competitive football programs, and everyone else goes under. That would be a tragedy."

College sports are important to Cruz and the fabric of the country, as the senator said. While football is the headlining sport in the Protect College Sports Act, everybody will be affected, hopefully in a positive way, with the bill.

"And so I think the reason Congress is going to happen is because college sports is too precious," Cruz said. "We've got to make sure this remains an avenue for opportunity for millions of kids, and we've got to make sure it remains not just football, but also all of women's sports, all of all of the non-revenue sports, all of the Olympic sports. This bill is designed to do all that."

title: “Stay Safe”: ESPN’s Laura Rutledge Gives Alarming Update for Texas-Ohio State Game as Calls Mount for Longhorns to Make Big Change

fullText:
Texas and Ohio State already have enough going on Saturday. No. 1 vs. No. 4, a packed house, and national attention. But fans are going to have to face another tough opponent. When ESPN's Laura Rutledge got to Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, she realized the heat was going to be part of the story.

"Look at this gorgeous place," Laura Rutledge said while showing the stadium. "It is extremely hot. Now, game time is going to be a little later than it is right now, but I think we're looking at about 100 degrees of kickoff tomorrow."

A fan of hers commented on the video,

"Laura, have fun tomorrow at the Texas vs Ohio State game in Austin,Texas and drink enough water Laura to stay hydrated please and thank you ???? stay safe and have fun at Austin,Texas tomorrow for the college football ???? game."

Texas Ohio State is going to be electric, but the Austin heat is a character of its own. 

Saturday's forecast calls for temperatures around 102 degrees, with the heat index potentially pushing above 100. The National Weather Service has issued a Heat Advisory for areas along and east of Interstate 35 from noon through 7 p.m. The kickoff is at 6:30 p.m.

Texas fans have already learned what that kind of afternoon can feel like. The season opener against Texas State was played at 2:30 p.m., with temperatures reaching 102 degrees and a heat index of 105. Austin-Travis County EMS transported 13 people from the stadium to hospitals, with three cases potentially heat-related. That experience left plenty of fans unimpressed with the idea of doing it all over again.

UT graduate student Alaiza Mata said she almost passed out. Another recalled people vomiting nearby and said some fans couldn't make it through the first half. Still, another student described the sun as something beyond ordinary Austin summer heat. Those stories are why Laura Rutledge's warning is getting attention before an even bigger crowd arrives. But the warning does not stop with the air temperature.

As Laura Rutledge noted, field temperatures at the stadium's artificial surface have reportedly climbed to roughly 160 degrees Fahrenheit during the hottest part of the day. That number opened a debate among Longhorn fans. Why is Texas still playing on synthetic turf?

One frustrated supporter wrote, "There is no good reason for Texas to have synthetic turf. A former Texas AD once arrogantly let us know they have more money than the Vatican. It should be mandatory as a member of the SEC to have all outdoor athletic facilities be natural grass." That argument probably was not going away after the turf-temperature report.

Another fan took a different approach, threatening to give up the seats rather than battle the weather again. "You're seriously making me consider selling my tix. Now taking bids. 2 seats on the 20 yd down low," they posted.

Then came the inevitable internet joke about cooking temperatures. "Isn't 160 a 'well done' cooking safe temp," one fan asked.

Not everybody is running for the exits, though. Some fans remember that the opener was even worse. "Last week on the field was hotter UT vs. TXST," one wrote.

And another summed up the attitude of the faithful. "Place is going to be rocking even with such suppressive heat," they commented.

That is probably the safest bet of the weekend. Texas-Ohio State is not the kind of game that empties a stadium. Still, Austin-Travis County EMS has plenty of reason to be cautious. Fans are being encouraged to drink water before arriving and throughout the day, wear lightweight clothing, use sunscreen, limit alcohol and caffeine, and step into shade or air conditioning whenever possible.

Starting hydration Friday night instead of trying to catch up Saturday is also recommended. The football will eventually take center stage. But Saturday begins with a different question. Can everyone handle the heat before Texas and Ohio State handle each other?

title: OSU Alum Kirk Herbstreit Gets Emotional on Full-Circle Moment 20 Years After Calling Ohio State-Texas Classic
description: Kirk Herbstreit has called the biggest games in college football history. He has sat in the booth for national championships, bitter rivalries, and playoff thrillers.
fullText:
Kirk Herbstreit has called the biggest games in college football history. He has sat in the booth for national championships, bitter rivalries, and playoff thrillers. Yet, certain games stay locked in his heart forever. Returning to Austin to call Ohio State against Texas is not just another assignment for him. It is a deeply personal walk down memory lane.

More than twenty years after Kirk Herbstreit called the 2005 Ohio State-Texas classic with Brent Musburger, he is walking back into Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium Saturday night to call the same matchup again. This time, Chris Fowler will be beside him. The OSU alum shared a clip from that 2005 broadcast on Instagram, and you could hear the memories coming through the caption.

"21 years ago almost to the day, #1 Ohio State @ #2 Texas met in week two of Saturday Night Football on ABC's debut season. Brent Musburger and I called the game and 21 years later… I'm calling the same matchup with @chrisfowler tomorrow night! Enjoy this flash from the past… Excited to see this matchup again soon!"

In 2005, Kirk Herbstreit was still building his broadcasting career. Ohio State arrived in Austin ranked No. 1, Texas was No. 2, and Vince Young was becoming one of the most dangerous players in the country. Troy Smith was running the Buckeyes' offense. Texas eventually won 25-22, finishing the night with a late touchdown that turned an already enormous game into a classic.

Ohio State and Texas have a way of delivering the biggest moments in college football. 

Kirk Herbstreit got another crack at the matchup a year later. Ohio State won that one 24-7 in Columbus. But maybe it's not the scoreboard that he remembers the most. Before that 2006 meeting, he was stunned by the number of Ohio State fans expected to make the trip to Texas.

Estimates reached 30,000 to 40,000 Buckeye fans, an absurd traveling crowd for a regular-season nonconference game at the time. Kirk Herbstreit also had a soft spot for those fans who packed their bags and followed Ohio State across the country.

"My favorite fans of Ohio State are those that go on the road," he said.

Two decades later, that traveling Buckeye army remains part of the show. And the game itself has somehow gotten even bigger. No. 1 Ohio State and No. 4 Texas meet Saturday night with both teams sitting at 1-0. This is the big one in the Big Ten-SEC showdown, with the two programs meeting again after two Buckeye wins.

That 2005 broadcast was the launchpad that turned Herbstreit from a promising young analyst into the undisputed voice of college football. Returning to the exact same press box two decades later carries immense personal weight, but the stakes on the field are just as massive.

With top-five rankings on the line and early College Football Playoff positioning hanging in the balance, this top-tier Big Ten SEC battle gives him the ultimate stage to celebrate how far both his career and this iconic national rivalry have come.

Ohio State took the last two, winning 28-14 in the CFP semifinal in the Cotton Bowl after the 2024 season. Then again, they beat Texas 14-7 in Columbus to start last season. Now Texas gets another shot, this time in Austin. The details are enough to make this one of the season's biggest games. Will Muschamp is taking over the Longhorns' defense, while Arthur Smith enters his first season directing the Buckeyes' offense.

There is no shortage of star power. Julian Sayin and Arch Manning headline the QB matchup. Jeremiah Smith remains the obvious problem for the Longhorns, although Texas has managed to handle him in the last two meetings. The Buckeye WR caught one pass for three yards in the playoff and six for 43 yards last season.

For Kirk Herbstreit, though, there is another layer. He was there when Ohio State-Texas first became appointment television. He watched thousands of Buckeye fans flood Austin. He has spent the years since becoming one of the most familiar voices in college football. Now he gets to call the matchup again inside the same stadium with the same two powerhouses. And that is what makes his full-circle moment feel a little bigger than just another Saturday night.

title: Outgoing Rep Chip Roy says the GOP has already 'delivered significantly,' but must 'finish the job'
description: Outgoing House Republican Chip Roy of Texas said that while Republicans have "delivered significantly," they still must "finish the job."
fullText:
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas — who lost the Lone Star State GOP attorney general primary runoff in May and will depart the U.S. House of Representatives when his current term expires — said Republicans have "delivered significantly" but "need to finish the job."

"Well, we've done so much that frankly, it kinda gets lost in a lot of the noise," Roy told Fox News Digital during an interview on Wednesday, pointing to issues such as tax provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump last year.

The Texan pointed to the nation's border as the "biggest example" of Republicans' achievements, saying that "we've literally shut down the flow across the border" through enforcing the law.

He also pointed to the passage of the "Laken Riley Act," a measure named after the 22-year-old woman murdered in 2024 by Jose Ibarra, a man who, according to a 2024 statement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), had previously been "arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)" after illegally entering the U.S., but was "paroled and released for further processing."

Roy said Republicans "need to unite with a singular vision about where we wanna take the country if we wanna be... rewarded in November... and then frankly looking ahead to 2028."

Texas Maga Battle Ends With Middleton Victory As Chip Roy Falls Short In Ag Race

"Have we done everything we should do? No," Roy said, claiming that "Congress has fallen short" regarding some of what they "should do."

But he still believes the GOP could potentially retain their majorities in both congressional chambers during the midterms.

"I think right now Republicans are staring at barely holding onto the Senate and slightly losing the House, but I still think we can win the House," he said.

The House is now only scheduled to work for several days next week before a lengthy break until after the Nov. 3 elections. Roy indicated that Republicans should get back to work after the midterms "to do our part to finish the job."

"Obviously I'm not campaigning. So I'm thinking a lot about what we could do with another reconciliation package or what we might be able to do in the lame duck or in January, when I'm not in office," he noted.

Fentanyl Deaths Could Now Cost Drug Dealers Their Lives Under New Gop Proposal

In a Sunday post on X, Roy wrote, "Government does not fund anything. It takes money from people under force of law and distributes it to other people very inefficiently and usually tyrannically. Child care is unaffordable because government (& corporate cronyism) has made life unaffordable. Stay out."

The New York Times reported last week that the Trump administration is moving to enable some married people with a stay-at-home parent situation to receive a childcare subsidy from a federal program that was meant to help parents who work.

The proposal "creates the option for a new category of care, parent-based child care, that will allow one married parent to receive C.C.D.F. [Child Care and Development Fund] assistance to care for their own child, while a spouse works at least 35 hours per week," the outlet reported, citing a draft document.

Roy said during the interview on Wednesday, "I just don't believe that it's good for the human soul to have the government coming in with a grant and making you dependent on government. I just don't philosophically think that that's freedom. I think freedom, non-dependence, independence is what makes America great."

A White House official said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Thursday that the Trump administration "has not announced any such proposal. Until and unless it does, any discussion about potential policies is baseless speculation."

Chip Roy Fields Proposal To Block Pay And Power For Longtime Lawmakers

As for whether he has any interest in running for office again, Roy said the matter is "up to God" and to Texans, adding that he has "a calling for service" and his current focus is on attempting to "solve the big problems for" Americans.

title: Shouts of ‘he should be shot’ heard during GOP midterm convention speech criticizing Democratic candidates
description: Shouts of “he should be shot” could be heard multiple times Thursday night at the Republican midterm convention as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz was criticizing prominent Democratic politicians by name.
fullText:
Shouts of "he should be shot" could be heard multiple times Thursday night at the Republican midterm convention as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz was criticizing prominent Democratic politicians by name.

Cruz mentioned three Democrats — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. After each name, there were shouts audible on the broadcast of "He should be shot!"

It was unclear if Cruz heard the shouts, and representatives for the senator and the Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

But the shouts came on the same day that many Republicans denounced political violence on the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Vice President JD Vance, who was friends with Kirk, reflected on his killing in a headlining speech.

El-Sayed responded during an interview on CNN's "The Source with Kaitlan Collins."

"I'm a dad with two daughters and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad," he told Collins. "This is what has become norm in our politics. I mean, literally calls to violence."

He added that "everybody who heard" the shouts should condemn them.

Kirk, the co-founder of Turning Point USA, was shot and killed on a Utah college campus a year ago. He was 31.

"Charlie was killed one year ago today," RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said as the second day of convention speeches kicked off. "He believed in America and freedom and young people's courage to stand up and fight for the country they love."

Many of Thursday's speeches were otherwise devoted to attacking Democrats as ideologically radical. The shouts of "He should be shot!" could be heard while Cruz was telling Republicans to take seriously the past comments and positions of Mamdani, El-Sayed and Talarico.

"A simple truth: When people tell you who they are, believe them," Cruz said. "When Mamdani says he wants to seize the means of production, he means it."

"When Abdul El-Sayed says he has a, quote, 'obligation,' to comply with Sharia law, he means it," the Texas senator said.

"And when James Talarico says he wants to dismantle capitalism, he means it," Cruz said.

Mamdani, a democratic socialist, spoke about "the end goal of seizing the means of production" during a 2021 speech discussing his political beliefs, according to Politifact. When the comment came up during his 2025 mayoral campaign, a spokesperson said his platform did not include seizing the means of production.

Cruz's criticism of El-Sayed stems from a 2009 interview with The New York Times where El-Sayed, then a medical student, said he felt an "obligation" to follow Sharia law in buying his first home. Muslims are discouraged from paying interest on loans, which can make seeking out a mortgage more complicated.

And Cruz was calling out Talarico over a recent CNN report that he said in 2020 that capitalism needed to be "dismantl(ed)" along with White supremacy and climate change. Talarico's campaign said the Democrat was a "proud capitalist" in response to the CNN story.

Cruz brought up Kirk's killing during his speech while denouncing what he described as a rising tide of extremism in politics, one day before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

"The hate that killed Charlie Kirk, that knocked down the Twin Towers, that led to two assassination attempts on President Trump, it just gets keeping getting worse and worse," Cruz said.

El-Sayed agreed in the CNN interview that politics was becoming too consumed by hate.

"When you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us," he said. "I hope that everybody who heard that is going to call it out for what it is: a call for violence that ought to be condemned across the board."

Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, the second highest-ranking Democrat in the House, condemned the shouts in an X post, saying "every single Republican" should as well. And Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, also weighed in, calling them "clear hate."

title: New poll rattles Texas governor's race as Election Day looms
description: Gina Hinojosa has pulled even with Gov. Greg Abbott at 47% in a new poll, wiping out a lead he held since spring. See where the governor's race stands.
fullText:
A new poll shows the Texas governor's race has swung to a dead heat — erasing the lead Gov. Greg Abbott had held over his Democratic challenger for months.

The N+ Univision Sept. 9 poll showed the Republican incumbent and Democrat Gina Hinojosa tied at 47%, with 5% undecided, and was released the day Republicans convened in Texas for their first midterm convention.

The poll also showed that Democrat state Rep. James Talarico has a narrow edge over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 48% to 43%, with 7% undecided in the Texas Senate race.

Here's a deeper dive into the poll for the Texas governor's race and where the race stands.

The poll was conducted from Aug. 27 to Sept. 4 and surveyed 1,000 registered voters in Texas. Because the poll was not a probability sample, it has no traditional margin of error; instead, the equivalent margin of error for a matched, propensity-score sampling design is plus or minus 3.6 percentage points.

Overall, the N+ Univision poll showed that since the 2024 election, Texas voters have shifted 8 points more toward Democrats, with 25% saying they have become more supportive of Democrats and 17% saying they have become more supportive of Republicans.

Among Hispanic voters, the shift is even larger, at 11 points. The single most-cited reason for changing views was President Donald Trump's actions as president, named by 25% of voters in the poll and 24% of Hispanic voters.

The poll also found that 44% of voters view Abbott favorably and 47% unfavorably, while 42% view Hinojosa favorably and 29% unfavorably.

Abbott also has a negative favorability rating among Hispanic voters, sitting at 41% to 50%.

The N+ Univision Sept. 9 poll follows a Texas Public Opinion Research Aug. 27 poll that showed Abbott pulling further ahead of Hinojosa, 49% to 42% with 6% undecided.

Last month, the Cook Political Report on Aug. 20 moved the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican" for several reasons.

But the report said it would adjust its findings as the race enters the final stretch to Election Day and once Abbott starts using attack ads to define Hinojosa — who the polls still show Texas voters are trying to get to know.

These two polls follow a summer of polls that showed the race between the two had been within the single digits:

Texas Politics Project (Aug. 25): 45% Abbott, Hinojosa 40%.

Texas Pulse (Aug. 7): Abbott 46%, Hinojosa 45%.

Texas Southern University (Aug. 4): Abbott 49%, Hinojosa 43%.

Texas Public Opinion Research (July 28): Abbott 45%, Hinojosa 42%.

New York Times (June 30): Abbott 51%, Hinojosa 44%.

Texas Politics Project (June 22): Abbott 47%, 40%.

title: Chip Roy on Trump dividends: ‘Dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms’
description: Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized President Trump’s Wednesday proposal to give every American adult a $5,000 dividend if the GOP wins the midterms, as other Republicans have also voiced skepticism ab...
fullText:
Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized President Trump's Wednesday proposal to give every American adult a $5,000 dividend if the GOP wins the midterms, as other Republicans have also voiced skepticism about the pledge.

"Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," Roy wrote Thursday on social platform X, pushing back on venture capitalist Clint Brown's defense of the president's proposal.

On Wednesday, the staunchly conservative Texan estimated that giving every American adult $5,000 would cost the federal government $1.2 trillion in fiscal 2027.

"Dear certain friends… deficits aside - you could almost ZERO out taxes for married parents of dependents up to $200,000 over 10 years!" Roy wrote on X.

Trump made the promise Wednesday, saying he will send the dividends to every adult citizen only if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate in November.

"Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," he said at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas.

There are roughly 270 million adults in the U.S. The president did not offer specifics on the proposal outside of saying recipients could only spend the money in the U.S.

"We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money," Trump remarked. "We don't want you going to China, to Germany."

It is unclear whether Congress would have to pass legislation approving the dividends. When the president proposed sending $2,000 tariff dividend checks to Americans last year, he claimed he didn't "believe" he needed congressional approval to do so. The tariff dividend checks proposal never came to fruition.

Trump made Wednesday's promise less than a month after the U.S. national debt crossed the $40 trillion threshold. The debt has increased by more than $3.8 trillion since the start of the president's second term.

Roy's estimated cost of the dividend is slightly less than the amount the federal government has paid in interest on the debt this fiscal year: $1.27 trillion. The U.S. government has paid more than $1 trillion in interest on the debt in each of the last three fiscal years.

Roy, who is departing Congress after losing the GOP primary runoff for Texas attorney general in May, was not alone among Republicans in opposing Trump's proposal.

Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) called the idea a "socialist vote-buying scheme" early Thursday morning.

"Sadly, most 'conservatives' don't even know (or care) that the president doesn't have the constitutional authority to spend $$, or send out 'dividend' checks without Congress," Good wrote later Thursday on X.

title: Talarico says he 'missed the mark' as he backtracks on controversial woke statements
description: James Talarico now backs banning transgender surgeries for minors and opposing trans athletes in girls' sports as the Texas Senate race heats up.
fullText:
In a Fox News exclusive interview, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico came out in favor of banning gender surgery for minors and opposed transgender-identifying men competing in women's sports.

Talarico also backtracked on several of his more controversial claims, including saying there are six genders and that "God is nonbinary."

This comes as the Texas Senate race, which is surprisingly close according to recent Fox News polling, enters its final months. The race is considered critical to both parties' chances of securing a Senate majority. Talarico is facing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican who has faced controversies of his own. A Republican loss in Texas would significantly impact President Donald Trump's ability to implement his agenda.

Fox News spoke with Talarico at a food drive campaign event in Dallas on Tuesday. Talarico's event took place as the first-ever GOP midterm convention kicked off just miles away in downtown Dallas.

Talarico Campaigns With Surgeon Who Operated On Transgender Minors: 'Wolf In Sheep's Clothing'

Asked whether he would vote as a U.S. senator in favor of a national ban on gender surgery for minors, Talarico answered, "Absolutely."

He said, "I've been consistent on this issue," explaining his opposition to a Texas bill to ban transgender surgeries on minors by saying the measure "was overly broad."

"If you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors," he said. "As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there's stuff in it that's really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole."

"It's why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do," he continued. "It's what I tried to do with that piece of legislation, and unfortunately, the amendment I supported was unsuccessful."

In 2023, as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico voted against a state bill titled SB 14, which prohibited certain gender surgery, puberty blockers and certain hormone treatments for minors. There were 18 amendments to the bill proposed by Democrats, all of which Talarico voted in favor and all of which ultimately failed.

In the same interview, Talarico acknowledged that men in women's sports is a significant issue in Texas. He said, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls' sports if it endangers safety or fairness."

"Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes. I care a lot about our students. And so, I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls' sports if it risks safety or fairness," he said.

Talarico's comments mark a shift from his earlier position as a Texas state lawmaker.

In 2021, while serving on the Texas House Public Education Committee, he opposed SB 29, which sought to require public-school athletes to compete based on the biological sex listed on their birth certificate, calling the issue a "manufactured problem." Later that year, he voted against HB 25, which enacted similar restrictions into Texas law.

James Talarico Admits Past Comments 'Missed The Mark' When Confronted On Claims Like God Is 'Non-binary'

He also addressed perhaps his most controversial statement, which he made in 2021, while opposing a Texas bill to keep men out of women's sports. Talarico said on the state House floor that "God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary."

"I was being provocative with that statement. I get that," Talarico admitted, explaining, "What I was trying to say is that you can't use human categories to define God, and that's not controversial theologically. In fact, the late Charlie Kirk, the late Pope Benedict all said the same thing."

Talarico continued, claiming "these comments are being clipped out of context to try to distract from Ken Paxton's career of corruption."

"You mentioned [Paxton] being acquitted in the state Senate. That was after two of his billionaire megadonors gave the lieutenant governor a $3 million check to buy his acquittal," Talarico said. "So, Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician in Texas, and he's gonna try to clip some of my comments, including comments where I was being a little provocative in order to try to distract from that career."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Paxton campaign for a response.

Longtime Gop Aide Defects To Dem Rising Star As Texas Senate Battle For Cornyn's Seat Heats Up

Regarding his past comment about there being more than two genders, Talarico said he does not currently believe there are six sexes.

"I've missed the mark on some of my past statements. I will be the first to admit it," he said. "What I meant is that there are two sexes, and then there's a small percentage of people with genetic abnormalities."

"Obviously didn't say it correctly. There are not six sexes. There are two, and I think the reason that politicians in that convention center across the street want to talk about six sexes is because they don't want to talk about $6 diesel," he said.

Though he walked back these controversies, Talarico did not hold back on his criticism of the Supreme Court, which he described as "infected" with corruption, saying it "needs to be overhauled."

He said that if elected, "You're going to expect that I will vote for overhaul to the Supreme Court. That will include binding codes of conduct for our justices. It'll include term limits, and I am open to a discussion about expanding the number of justices."

Following these controversies, Talarico pledged to keep his message focused on affordability for the remainder of the campaign.

"Everywhere I go across the state of Texas, people are struggling to survive in this economy. They are struggling to afford the basics: groceries, gas, utilities, healthcare. And that's what I'm going to be focused on from now until Election Day."

On the topic of affordability, Talarico said that "we should not have a state income tax" in Texas. This is despite Talarico previously voting against a measure to permanently ban a state income tax, which he suggested was redundant and an example of "government waste at its worst."

The measure was ultimately passed by the Texas Legislature and approved by Texas voters in November 2019.

More than 1.7 million free eggs have already been delivered to Texas food banks, with another 5.3 million slated to arrive in the coming weeks as part of an antitrust settlement with three major egg producers, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday.

Under the agreements, the companies will donate more than 7 million eggs to Texas food banks and pay a combined $3.3 million to participating states.

"After securing 7 million eggs for the people of Texas, I am excited to announce that Texans will now have an opportunity to receive cartons of free eggs in communities across the state," Paxton said. Other participating food banks are located across the state, including Austin, San Antonio, Tyler, Corpus Christi, El Paso, Laredo, Odessa, Pharr, Beaumont, Amarillo, Lubbock, Victoria, Abilene and Wichita Falls.

BOSTON (AP) — Zach Neto hit a three-run homer over the Green Monster, Ryan Johnson gave up three runs over six innings and the Los Angeles Angels beat the Boston Red Sox 6-4 on Wednesday night to take the series.

Jose Siri added a two-run shot and Denzer Guzman a long solo homer for the Angels, who won consecutive games for the first time since taking three straight against Texas on Aug. 11-13.

Winning for just the fourth time in 15 games, Los Angeles captured its first road series since taking two of three from Houston on Aug. 18-20.

Roman Anthony hit a two-run homer and Wilyer Abreu a solo one for Boston, which lost the final two games after winning the opener Monday.

Coming in with a 1.67 ERA in his last six starts when he gave zero or one run five times, Johnson (4-8) breezed through his four scoreless innings, giving up two singles while his teammates built a 6-0 lead.

Jake Bennett (9-7) gave up a season-high six runs — five coming in one inning to surpass his previous high of four — on nine hits in 5 1/3 innings.

Ben Joyce got the final three outs for his fourth save despite giving up a run.

title: Appeals Court Grants Immunity to Texas Cops Who Held Handcuffed Woman Face Down in a Fire Ant Hill
description: The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Taylor Rogers didn't show that it was clearly established that it was excessive force to be held down on a pile of fire ants while handcuffed.
fullText:
A federal appeals court ruled that a Texas woman can't sue two Santa Fe police officers who pinned her face down on a fire ant hill while she was handcuffed, causing her to receive hundreds of painful bites to her face.

In an August 6 opinion, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed a lower court decision allowing Taylor Rogers' lawsuit against the City of Santa Fe and the two officers to move forward. Instead, the panel held that the officers were shielded from her claims under the doctrine of qualified immunity.

In a press conference last Friday, Rogers' attorney, Randy Kallinen, criticized the ruling.

"The United States 5th Circuit Court of Appeals is out of touch with the Constitution and the public, granting police immunity in the most egregious of cases," Kallinen said. "The people need to elect officials who will nominate and affirm judges loyal to the Constitution."

Kallinen told The Daily News that he has requested an en banc hearing for the full 15-member 5th Circuit to review the case, and he'll petition the Supreme Court for review if that fails.

"The facts, injuries and footage speaks for itself," Kallinen said. "If they let this one slide, they're letting police do just about anything."

Santa Fe Independent School District Police officers arrested Rogers in 2021 after she drove erratically through a school parking lot and disobeyed commands to stop. According to the 5th Circuit opinion, she continued to thrash and resist officers in a state of hysteria after being handcuffed.

Santa Fe ISD officer Christian Carranza then threw Rogers to the ground and held her face down in a pile of fire ants while twisting her legs upward, effectively hog-tying her.

Body camera footage released by Kallinen showed Rogers begging for Carranza to stop while multiple other officers watched. "Ants are on my face! Ants are getting on my face, please!" Rogers yelled. "How can y'all do this? Ants are on my face! Please let go!"

After pleading guilty to felony evading arrest, Rogers filed a civil rights lawsuit in 2023 alleging excessive force, failure to intervene, cruel and unusual punishment, and deprivation of due process. Pictures accompanying Rogers' lawsuit showed her face, neck, and upper chest covered with hundreds of ant bites.

"No reasonable officer would have held Ms. Rogers legs up and behind her body whilst also pressing her face and torso into a pile of fire ants," Rogers' lawsuit said, noting that she is 5 feet, 7 inches tall and weighs roughly 130 pounds.

However, the officers argued they were entitled to qualified immunity, a legal doctrine that makes government officials immune from lawsuits when the constitutional right they are accused of violating isn't clearly established.

Last June, a federal judge allowed Rogers' lawsuit to proceed and ruled that the two Santa Fe officers weren't entitled to qualified immunity.

The 5th Circuit panel reversed that decision, ruling that because Rogers couldn't point to analogous case law finding that using a leg-leverage technique to restrain a resisting suspect on top of a fire ant hill was unconstitutional excessive force, her claims were barred by qualified immunity.

Civil liberties groups and criminal justice advocates have long argued that qualified immunity allows police officers to drag out lawsuits for years and stop cases from ever being considered by jury, even in cases of egregious abuse, such as detectives lying under oath or correctional officers who watched a jail inmate die soaked in his own vomit over the course of 13 hours.

title: Kudlow to Cruz: ‘You might want to think’ about announcing presidential bid in November
description: Fox Business host Larry Kudlow on Tuesday told Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) that he “might want to think” about launching a bid for the presidency in November. Kudlow asked the Texas senator about whether ...
fullText:
Fox Business host Larry Kudlow on Tuesday told Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) that he "might want to think" about launching a bid for the presidency in November.

Kudlow asked the Texas senator about whether or not he will run for the Republican nomination for president in 2028 in an appearance on the host's show.

"So, what I will say is there will be plenty of time to have that conversation after the midterms," Cruz answered. "We're less than 60 days out from the midterms, so my focus –– if we lose the House and Senate, all the legislative progress we have grinds to a halt, and it is two years of warfare against President Trump and his agenda."

Kudlow noted how Trump declared his candidacy right after the 2022 midterms and credited that to his success in 2024.

"I'm just putting it out there," he said. "You might want to think about it. I mean, right after he did that, a lot of people scratched their heads, and it turns out that was a close outbid. It really was."

Cruz previously ran for president in 2016 and at one point was seen as a front-runner. He won 11 state contests, including the Iowa caucuses, before suspending his campaign as Trump built a large delegate lead.

The Texan eventually backed President Trump in the general election, though he did not endorse him at the GOP's convention in Cleveland that summer, and was then booed by Trump supporters.

At the time, Cruz reportedly told allies that he thought there was something "fundamentally wrong" with evangelical voters backing Trump. Then-candidate Trump threatened to "spill the beans" on Cruz's wife, Heidi Cruz, and reposted an unflattering photo of her compared with one of first lady Melania Trump, and he claimed there was "voter fraud" in his loss to Cruz in Iowa.

The Texas senator is seen as a Republican contender for president in 2028 and has said the GOP has not coalesced around Vice President Vance as the party's presidential nominee.

"There's going to be a full discussion about who we are and what we believe," Cruz told MS NOW's Ali Vitali late last month when asked if the party has settled on Vance.

Cruz added that the GOP was in "the midst of a debate about who our party is," noting that there will be "time to figure" out his role in that future.

Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who ran against Cruz and Trump in 2016, are seen as favorites to possibly succeed Trump. Neither has said publicly whether they will run in 2028, but both of their names are mentioned as potential GOP contenders.

A recent Emerson College poll showed Rubio outperforming Vance in multiple hypothetical 2028 presidential match-ups against Democratic candidates.

title: Jeremiah Smith has been quiet against Texas. Can Ohio State get him going in rematch?
description: Some incredible numbers show how much Texas has limited Ohio State star wide receiver Jeremiah Smith in the past. Will that continue in 2026?
fullText:
Jeremiah Smith has presented opponents with matchup nightmares since arriving at Ohio State, overwhelming defensive backs with his size and speed.

But in each of the past two years, Texas has kept him in check.

Between the 2025 season opener and the teams' earlier meeting in the College Football Playoff semifinals, Smith has combined for just seven receptions for 46 yards.

The modest production looms large ahead of their rematch in Austin on Sept. 12, as the Buckeyes look for ways to maximize the impact of their superstar receiver, arguably the best player in college football.

"It's no mystery that when the ball is in his hands, good things happen," Ohio State coach Ryan Day said.

While Day said the Buckeyes would work to make sure Smith is a major factor against the Longhorns, he has hardly been an afterthought in previous game plans. Texas has just sold out to stop him.

The Longhorns devoted significant attention to Smith in both games, using deep zone coverages to keep him from beating them over the top.

When they held Smith to one catch for 3 yards in the playoff semifinals, safety Michael Taaffe floated toward his side of the field to help in coverage.

Smith has not caught a pass deeper than 7 yards downfield against the Longhorns. Even as quarterback Julian Sayin found Smith touches last season, it was largely a mix of screens, curls and other short routes to the flats. The average depth of Smith's 10 targets was a mere 3.7 yards, according to Pro Football Focus.

Smith also had two uncharacteristic drops against Texas last season, and he was still in the early stages of building chemistry with Sayin, who was in his debut as Ohio State's starting quarterback.

"There were opportunities where I could have taken the ball toward him," Sayin said. "I wouldn't say they limited him in any aspect."

The most glaring instance was on a fourth-and-1 at midfield on the Buckeyes' opening drive. Sayin found tight end Max Klare toward the sideline, but Smith was open streaking downfield, having burst through a seam. Klare dropped the pass. One to Smith might have produced a touchdown.

Sayin and Smith were on the same page when the Buckeyes opened their season last weekend with a 56-3 win over Ball State. Smith caught eight passes for 151 yards and two touchdowns in the first half alone. He rested in the second half as the game grew lopsided, with Ohio State anticipating this week's trip to Texas for a top-five matchup.

It remains to be seen how much Texas will follow the same approach after hiring Will Muschamp as defensive coordinator to replace Pete Kwiatkowski, who was fired by coach Steve Sarkisian in December after five seasons with the Longhorns.

Muschamp has not been a primary defensive coordinator since he was at Auburn in 2015, adding a new variable to the series with the uncertainty over how the Longhorns will evolve under his direction. The unknown has Day's attention, as he acknowledged the limits to their pregame preparations. The Buckeyes will likely need to adjust after the ball is snapped.

"But we know that there will be a plan to stop Jeremiah," Day said, "try to identify what that is and then have the plans in place for what that looks like."

Day said Sayin will have a significant role in helping to identify Texas' tendencies in game, a situation in which his year of starting experience could pay dividends.

"He's got to recognize what's going on and respond from there," Day said. "All those things are part of our conversation as we put our game plan together."

For as much as Texas has contained Smith, it has not been Ohio State's undoing. The Buckeyes won both meetings.

The Longhorns' devotion to Smith allowed Carnell Tate to emerge as a weapon. Tate was the Buckeyes' leading receiver in both games, combining for nine catches for 136 yards and a touchdown.

Tate's 40-yard scoring haul in last year's 14-7 win gave the Buckeyes a commanding lead early in the fourth quarter.

"What makes a great player great is he makes everybody on the field better," Day said, "and certainly Jeremiah does that."

With Tate having left for the NFL, the Buckeyes have a new cast of receivers poised to benefit from the attention devoted to Smith, a group led by UTSA transfer Devin McCuin and returning slot receiver Brandon Inniss.

Ohio State defensive end Kenyatta Jackson Jr. said he has never seen an opponent contain Smith to this degree. Even when they were high school teammates years earlier at Chaminade-Madonna in Hollywood, Florida, Smith dominated defenses.

"Every team we went against, he put 150-plus on them," Jackson said.

But Jackson said Smith has handled the frustrations against Texas well.

"He wants to make plays for sure," Jackson said, "but as long as the team wins, he's OK with it. That's the type of person he is."

Labeling Smith "arguably the best player in college football," Texas coach Steve Sarkisian spoke at length to the media on Sept. 7 about the Ohio State wide receiver.

"I think, one, he garners your attention and he deserves our attention," Sarkisian said. "... The challenge is, with him, it's the size, speed, catch radius. He's a big, physical guy who can cover a lot of ground in a short amount of time. It doesn't always look like it, but it almost feels like it. You can feel his presence on the field.

"... This guy looks like Julio Jones. This guy looks like A.J. Brown physically. He can cover ground and then, because he's so strong, 50-50 catches are difficult with him. You have to have a plan. But I think like anything when you have a plan against somebody like him, you can't just throw all fastballs. As good as a fastball as you have, if that's all you got, sooner or later you're gonna hit it. We've got to be able to mix our pitches up in how we defend him and how we defend the scheme."

Staff reporter Dan Aulbach contributed to this report.

title: Texas education board approves controversial curriculum changes tying 'radical Islam' to 9/11 attacks
description: The Texas Board of Education gave final approval to controversial social studies changes impacting how students learn about Islam and Christianity.
fullText:
The Texas Board of Education gave final approval to changes to the state's high school social studies curriculum, a controversial move that will impact how students are taught about Islam and Christianity.

The amended social studies curriculum, which covers U.S. history, government and world geography, comes after dozens of people gave public testimony, with most expressing their opposition to the finalized version.

The board approved language asserting that "radical Islam" motivated the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks rather than taking a more narrow focus on the terrorist groups involved in the attack.

The material also requires students to study early Islam through Prophet Muhammad's "brutal military campaigns against Jewish and Christian tribes," the "normalization of slavery" and the taking of female captives as "harem slaves."

Nba Champion Josh Hart Celebrates Texas Board Of Education's Vote To Make Bible Passages Required Reading

Several Democratic State Board of Education members pushed back against the wording, but the Republican-majority board still approved that section and the other changes on Friday.

Muslim groups and students, as well as multiple curriculum experts, also spoke out against the new changes.

"I feel attacked, as if my religion doesn't belong," Habiiba Quresh, a 15-year-old Muslim student, told the board, according to The Texas Tribune. "I shouldn't have to defend my religion in the middle of history class because of one sentence someone on this board wrote."

At least three of the board-appointed curriculum experts also warned against the new language.

Ted Cruz, Conservatives Respond After Talarico Criticizes Bible-related Education In Schools As 'Propaganda'

Andrea Hutchison, a social studies curriculum coordinator for Prosper ISD, argued the material did not "hold up to close historical scrutiny," according to the outlet. Robert Koons, a philosophy professor at UT-Austin, said most nonreligious scholars find the source of the claims "not very reliable," adding that he would warn against including material that is "not based on well-established secular sources."

The Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations said the board's decision to "single out and denigrate Islam, minimize the brutal realities of slavery and segregation, and entirely erase Palestinian history is an affront to our system of education and the First Amendment."

"No credible scholar of history validates the bigoted caricatures of Islam this curriculum teaches," CAIR Texas and CAIR Action Texas said in a joint statement. "Even the board's own appointed experts warned it doesn't hold up to historical scrutiny, yet the board voted against removing it. Texas students of every background deserve an education that tells the truth about their history and their neighbors' history, not propaganda that teaches them to see each other as threats or erases them from the story altogether."

State Board of Education Chair Aaron Kinsey pushed back on criticism of the revised standards, saying opponents had "sensationalize[d] all these topics and [made] them seem more divisive than they actually are." He added that board members "worked through, democratically, how to make those choices on behalf of our constituents" and said he believed they "did an exceptional job overall."

But Republican school board member Julie Pickren boasted about the material's final approval, according to Fox 7.

"This social studies law that got us here, I've been working on for over 10 years with the House and the Senate, the Texas House and Texas Senate ... and so this is such a huge accomplishment; this vote kind of bookends 12 years of life's work," Pickren said.

The approved curriculum is expected to be phased into classrooms during the 2030-31 school year.

When blitzed, Reed earned a solid 78.0 passing grade, making quick decisions to check down to the flat or use his legs to prevent a negative play. fullText:
Texas A&M's offensive line struggled during the first half of Saturday's 50-0 shutout win over Missouri State, but improved in the second half, much to starting quarterback Marcel Reed's liking, as third-year coach Mike Elko and OL coach Adam Cushing made the necessary adjustments, leading to better communication at the LOS while paying close attention to their assignments.

At left tackle, LSU transfer Tyree Adams earned the third-highest Pro Football Focus grade (79.3) and was highly impressive in pass protection and run blocking, which is very important heading into Saturday's home matchup vs. Arizona State, while junior left guard Blake Ivy should retain his starting job, as his first-half struggles disappeared after halftime.

These blocking issues, after watching the tape a second time, stemmed from missed assignments, which was expected in the first game of the season after replacing four starters from the 2025 unit. Depth-wise, Elko could have certainly made drastic changes, but chose to stick with most of his original starting rotation, including South Carolina transfer right guard Trovon Baugh, who also struggled.

After the game, Marcel Reed discussed his close relationship with all his offensive linemen, including right tackle Wilkin Formby, Tyree Adams, and Blake Ivy, whose bond should help this revamped group protect their quarterback and play much better football for the rest of the season.

"I remember running out, and Wilkin Formby just said, 'I love you, brother.' I said, 'I love you, too.' Tyree Adams was checking in on me. I saw Blake Ivy maul somebody and get hype. They're going to protect me."

Mentality is everything as an offensive lineman, knowing that your central job is to keep the quarterback clean and open up holes in the running game. It's up to Adam Cushing to do his job and fix these remaining issues, which could lead to a change in the lineup, but right now, the second-half improvement shows this group is poised to improve.

"They said more to me. They tried to lift me up. Respect those guys a lot and the care they have for their quarterbacks. Those guys want to protect. I know they will get it done each Saturday."
